planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Silver King tolerates urban conditions, salt spray, and heat well, making it a reliable upright evergreen for difficult sites.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Silver King is adaptable to poor soils, heat, pollution, and salty coastal conditions once established. This upright, densely branched evergreen cultivar bears midsize, oval, scalloped-edged leaves in gray-green overlaid with thick, silvery-cream margins, providing a bright, variegated accent year-round. Small, inconspicuous cream flowers appear in spring but are not the plant's main ornamental feature. Its narrow, columnar-tending habit makes it a good choice for screening, hedging, informal borders, or trained as a container topiary specimen. Shear or prune as needed in spring to maintain shape; watch for euonymus scale, which can be a problem on stressed plants in humid climates.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Sunspot needs some direct sun to develop and hold its gold leaf centers, which fade toward green in deep shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where it will get at least some direct sun to keep its gold variegation bright. Sunspot arose as a sport of 'Emerald Cushion' and is distinguished from most variegated Euonymus fortunei cultivars by its reversed pattern: a bold golden-yellow blotch fills the center of each glossy, dark-green-margined leaf, rather than the more common cream or white leaf edge. It grows as a low, dense, mounding shrub wider than tall, useful as a bright groundcover, bank cover, or low foundation planting, and like other wintercreeper cultivars will also climb if given a wall or trellis to cling to. It is tough and drought-tolerant once established but is susceptible to euonymus scale, so monitor plantings in humid climates and treat promptly if scale appears.

common_name: Lawrence Crocker Daphne (Dwarf Fragrant Rock Garden Daphne)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or early spring in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; this slow-growing dwarf daphne resents root disturbance, so choose a permanent raised-bed or rock-garden site from the start.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade, ideally in a raised bed or rock garden where drainage around the crown is excellent year-round. Lawrence Crocker is a dwarf hybrid daphne named for a founder of Siskiyou Rare Plant Nursery, believed to be a cross between Daphne arbuscula and Daphne collina. It forms a dense, slow-growing, rounded mound under two feet tall, smothered in spring with intensely fragrant, deep pink flowers, often with a lighter rebloom scattered through summer. Because it stays so compact, it suits troughs, raised beds, and small-space rock gardens where larger daphnes would be out of scale. Avoid wet, heavy soils and disturbance to the root zone, both of which this genus tolerates poorly; all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Briggs Moonlight Daphne (Golden Variegated Burkwood Daphne)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Briggs Moonlight is grown chiefly for its luminous creamy-ivory and green variegated foliage, with fragrant pale pink spring flowers as a secondary feature.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; like other Burkwood daphnes, it resents transplanting once established, so choose a permanent site at planting time. Briggs Moonlight bears striking foliage with luminous, creamy-ivory leaf centers bordered by narrow green margins, a showier and more strongly variegated sport in the same group as the familiar 'Carol Mackie'. In mid-spring it produces clusters of small, fragrant, pale pink flowers, though the variegated foliage remains the main attraction through the whole growing season. Its compact, rounded habit suits a border, entry planting, or foundation bed where the foliage can be appreciated up close. Avoid heavy pruning and waterlogged soil, both poorly tolerated by this genus; all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Drops of Gold Japanese Holly (Golden-Variegated Compact Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; foliage color develops best with at least several hours of direct sun, fading toward green in deeper shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, giving it the brightest light available to develop its signature coloring. Drops of Gold is a patented, uniquely variegated female Japanese holly whose outermost and uppermost small, glossy, rounded leaves mature to bright golden yellow, grading inward and downward to softer yellow-green and rich green on interior and shaded foliage, giving the whole shrub a two-toned, gilded appearance. Broad and upright in habit, it fills in as a bright hedge, foundation planting, or specimen accent, and like other Japanese hollies tolerates shearing well if a more formal shape is wanted. Being female, it can produce small black fruit in fall if a male Ilex crenata grows nearby, though it is primarily grown for foliage color rather than fruit.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in shade to partial shade; Greensprite is a larger-growing, more vigorous selection of coast leucothoe than the straight species, eventually forming a wide, arching mound.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, highly acidic soil in shade to partial shade, allowing generous room for its eventual wide spread. Greensprite is a selection of coast leucothoe valued for its graceful, arching branches clothed in narrow, willow-like, glossy evergreen leaves that take on a reddish-bronze cast in winter. In spring it bears small, white, urn-shaped flowers in drooping racemes along the undersides of the stems, typical of the heath family. It ultimately grows considerably larger and wider than the species type, making it useful as a sprawling shade-garden filler, bank cover, or naturalistic mass planting beneath trees where its arching habit has room to spread. It is notably deer resistant and, once established, needs little more than routine moisture during dry spells and occasional thinning of old canes at the base.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; Pabella is a female-flowering sport of 'Rubella' selected for a sturdier, more upright habit than older female skimmia cultivars, and needs a male pollinator such as 'Rubella' or 'Kew Green' nearby to set fruit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade. Pabella arose as a naturally occurring female-flowered mutation found on the widely grown male cultivar 'Rubella', and was selected for its bushier, sturdier, more upright growth compared to older, sometimes sprawling or procumbent female skimmia cultivars. Fragrant panicles of small white flowers open in spring from attractive buds, followed on pollinated plants by glossy green berries that ripen to bright red and persist through winter for strong cold-season interest. Because it is female, plant it near a male skimmia such as 'Rubella' or 'Kew Green' to ensure good fruit set. It thrives in deeper shade than most berrying evergreens, making it valuable for a shaded foundation bed or woodland garden where few other shrubs offer winter fruit display.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Plant Breeders' Rights register

common_name: White Dwarf Skimmia (Compact Male Pollinator Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in shade to partial shade; White Dwarf is a compact male selection grown as a fragrant pollinator and does not set berries itself.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in shade to partial shade, where it tolerates heavier shade than most flowering evergreens. White Dwarf, sold under the cultivar name 'Moerings 1', is a compact, slow-growing male skimmia staying smaller than standard male cultivars such as 'Kew Green', with glossy, aromatic, leathery leaves and clusters of small, fragrant, yellow-green buds opening to white flowers in spring. As a male clone it produces no berries, but is valued for its tidy size in small gardens and containers and for its ability to pollinate nearby female skimmia cultivars grown for their red winter fruit. Water during dry spells, mulch to keep soil evenly moist and acidic, and prune only lightly to remove dead or crossing growth.

common_name: Sunset Boulevard Nandina (Coral-to-Red Compact Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sunset Boulevard develops its richest coral and burgundy tones with more direct sun exposure and cold winter temperatures.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sunset Boulevard is a compact, upright nandina selection bred for wider-than-typical leaflets and continuously shifting foliage color through the seasons. New growth emerges pale coral-pink, matures to light yellow-green through summer, then intensifies into rich red and burgundy tones as temperatures cool in fall and winter, giving the shrub an ever-changing, sunset-like palette year-round. Its dense, upright habit works well in mixed borders, foundation plantings, and mass plantings where season-long foliage color is more important than flowers or fruit. It is drought- and heat-tolerant once established and needs only minimal pruning to maintain its naturally neat form.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Tama-ryu Mondo Grass (Dwarf Mounding Mondo Grass)

planting.note: Plant small divisions or plugs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Tama-ryu is a dwarf, slow-spreading selection intermediate in size between standard mondo grass and the tiniest miniature forms like 'Kyoto Dwarf'.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping newly set plugs consistently watered while they knit together into a mat. Tama-ryu is a Japanese dwarf selection of mondo grass forming dense, low, rounded tufts of narrow, dark green, grass-like foliage, larger and faster to fill in than the diminutive 'Kyoto Dwarf' but still noticeably more compact and mounding than standard mondo grass. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a tidy, fine-textured carpet, making it useful for edging shaded paths, filling gaps between stepping stones, and underplanting in Japanese-style and woodland gardens. It is evergreen, deer resistant, and tolerates light foot traffic once established; division of mature clumps is the most practical way to propagate and expand a planting.
